headline: New York Library Races to Digitize Century of Decaying Film and Sound
meta_description: Engineers at the New York Public Library are digitizing irreplaceable recordings and films before they decay beyond recovery, preserving cultural history for f…
summary_short: A team of preservation specialists in a Lincoln Center basement is rescuing decades of film, tape, and audio recordings from decay, making history accessible to all.
body:
Beneath Lincoln Center, media preservation engineer Rhony Dostaly describes his work as operating a time machine. He and colleagues at the New York Public Library are racing against chemical decay to digitize over a century of sound and moving images stored on film, tape, discs, and cylinders—materials that are deteriorating rapidly while the machines that play them vanish from existence. Once digitized, most material will be accessible to anyone with a library card, ensuring that moments captured by figures like Harry Belafonte and Malcolm X, along with recordings like the UN Radio Division's 1949 New Year's Day broadcast, survive for future generations.

The urgency is stark. Acetate film suffers from "vinegar syndrome," a chemical decay that leaves it brittle and warped with no possibility of reversal. Audiotape arrives crinkled and stuck together, requiring hand repair described by engineer Victoria Fajardo as "kind of like surgery." Even supposedly robust Digital Betacam cassettes have begun to shed, forcing specialist Francis Dougherty to clean his playback deck between tapes. "Every year this job gets more difficult," he said. "Every year physical media degrades."

The crisis extends beyond the material itself. Fewer technicians remain who can repair or maintain the specialized machines needed for playback. Universities train young specialists, but with equipment increasingly rare, hands-on experience is disappearing. Innovators like California engineer Nick Bergh are building custom machines—including optical turntables and laser-aligned playback systems—to read damaged recordings without physical contact. The paradox, according to archivist Jeffrey Willens, is that as playback technology improves, the original recordings keep deteriorating. Every year of delay means irreplaceable heritage lost forever.
quick_facts: New York Public Library digitizes film, tape, and recordings over 100 years old
Acetate film suffers 'vinegar syndrome'—irreversible chemical decay
UN Radio disc from 1949 preserved using custom-built optical turntable
Fewer technicians worldwide can repair original playback machines
Work marked by UN's World Day for Audiovisual Heritage (October 27)
